utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you hear the proceedings, follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can hear you well and I understand the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers Office of the Prosecution. With me today is co-counsel, Ms. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager is Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. Good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. Vasvija Vidovic and John Jones for the Defence of Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us this morning our legal assistants, Ms. Adisa Mehic, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No preliminaries on the side of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. I think I can give the floor to Mr. Di Fazio to conclude on his part of the closing arguments for the Prosecution. Take your time, Mr. Di Fazio. We are not in a hurry. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. I will stop shortly, after concluding this part of my submissions, but I will make a small guest appearance later in the day following Ms. Richardson's submissions, and that will be on the issue of witnesses and how to treat their evidence, the issue of hostile witnesses that was raised by the Defence. But if I can return now to matters that I was addressing you on yesterday, just a couple of things from yesterday. The reference to Mustafa Salihovic being -- said to be the note taker of P84, if Your Honours please, is at the transcript in T-8967 to 68. One other matter that I wanted to raise to you about P84 is concerning its subjectivity or objectivity, is the fact that it was certified at the back of the document. That in itself is evidence that it was intended to be some sort of official document. You'll find the certification at the very back of the document. And that also lends weight to the submission that it was not a document riddled with subjectivity or useless because of subjective input. The other matter that I very briefly wanted to raise with you, it's perhaps a little obvious, but it needs to be made, it's, of course, not just documents that support documents that are uncommented upon. It's other evidence in the case. Nothing illustrates it better than the example of the document raised by my colleague, Ms. Sellers, yesterday. That was P25. That's, I believe uncommented on, and I believe has no chain of custody. Yet the accused himself, as Ms. Sellers pointed out to you yesterday, commented on the document itself. That is a document that the Defence complains has shortcomings because it was never shown to a witness. Well, you can see that's an example of how evidence in the case can simply take care of that consideration completely in certain circumstances. So it's not just documents supporting each other, it's other evidence as well. Can I turn now to the issue of forensic evidence? Yesterday I made some submissions to you on the -- what I submit was the more cautious and moderate approach of the -- Dr. Fagel and Dr. Kerzan when compared to the evidence of Professor Bilic. Just by way of illustration, let's just look very briefly at P75. You don't need to look at the actual content of it. That's the document dated the 26th of May and is an expansion of the Srebrenica TO Staff from seven to ten members so it comes -- it's created on the face of it very shortly after that all important Bajramovici meeting. That was objected to by the Defence. It was emphatically declared by Professor Bilic not to be by Naser Oric. You can see -- you can see it in -- I believe it's annex B to the Prosecution's final brief, which sets out all of the results of, inter alia, amongst other things, of documents that were examined by all three experts and you can see the results there. Highly probable according to Fagel, not by Naser Oric, according to Professor Bilic; written by Naser Oric, according to Dr. Kerzan. This is also a document from the Sokolac collection as well. So that deals a double blow, firstly to any suggestion of conspiracy or the work of a seasoned Serb forger and secondly -- sorry, I withdraw that. It certainly deals a blow to that conspiracy theory. And secondly, of course, it's a very damaging document because of the actual content itself. The Prosecution expert, Dr. Fagel was in the Prosecution's submission probably the best placed of all the experts, handwriting experts, to give you in -- opinions. His qualifications were clearly impressive. His own qualifications, his experience, and his ongoing contact with other experts in the field. He had no rational or explicable reason to colour his conclusions or to be influenced by consideration -- other, outside considerations in reaching his conclusions. And most importantly of all, he had a really good range of known signatures, the best of all three experts, to use as his tool in comparing the questioned signatures. He had, I can't recall off the top of my head now, but over 30, if I recall, known signatures of Naser Oric to use in coming to his conclusions, which is far better than both Kerzan and Bilic. Far better. And it permitted him to have a far better view of natural variation in the signatures and, of course, natural variation is, in the Prosecution's submission, the sort of thing, the sort of features that Professor Bilic hung his hat on. The dot, you recall the dot, and the distance of loops and so on from other structures in the signature and so on. So he was able to observe, as I said, far greater variation. He's in a far better position to be able to tell you whether something is the result of the forger's lack of skill or whether it's natural variation. It's something that is important in the Prosecution's submission. Coming back to P75, it also is relevant to the issue of the Hamdija Fejzic signatures. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If you accept the evidence of Dr. Fagel and Dr. Kerzan on P75, namely that it's Naser Oric's signature or extremely likely to be Naser Oric's signature, then it -- the conclusion of Professor Bilic that the other signature that appears on P75, namely that conclusion that it's a forged signature or not the signature of Hamdija Fejzic, carries far less weight in the Prosecution's submission. It's most unlikely in the Prosecution's submission that you'd have the juxtaposition of one known -- one genuine signature, this is if you accept the two experts. I say you should. But it's very unlikely that you have them both together -- forgery and -- or it's just not explicable or comprehensible reason why that should be so. And in the Prosecution's submission, if you -- as I said, if you accept the evidence of Kerzan and Fagel, that's going to throw a lot of doubt, should cause you a lot of misgivings about the other body of evidence of Dr. -- Professor Bilic, about the Fejzic signatures. Finally on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, would you accept that any case of any expert, calligraphic expert or handwriting or signature expert, that expert notwithstanding his or her expertise, could be completely right in some conclusions and absolutely wrong in others? MR. DI FAZIO: As a matter of a possibility, I would have to, as a matter of reason, accept that. Not just a handwriting expert, any expert in any given field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the moment we are talking about handwriting experts. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. In the case of handwriting experts, I can't suggest to you that that is a matter much impossibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to understand what your position is. As regards Fagel and Kerzan, I think we completely understand what you are submitting. In regard to Professor Bilic, are you submitting that all his findings should be ignored? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. I'm submitting that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even considering the difference in the burden of proof between the Prosecution and the Defence when it comes to authenticity of documents? MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what Your Honours are saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, if the situation obtains where Professor Bilic has examined this exhibit, which neither Mr. Kerzan and/or Mr. Fagel or Mr. Koeijer have examined and he's come to a specific conclusion, are you submitting that because, according to you, Fagel and Kerzan are more reliable than Professor Bilic is, therefore, logical or -- logical conclusion should be that all Professor Bilic's findings ought to be thrown overboard when the burden that the Defence has in that regard if they take it upon themselves to prove that a particular document is forged or is not authentic, theirs -- the burden of proof is not like yours. MR. DI FAZIO: No. I understand that, Your Honours. I appreciate that and that's a very valid point. All I can say is this is a common problem that all courts face when they have experts of competing views and unfortunately courts are charged with having to make decisions about that sort of evidence. Now, if you can't dismiss what Bilic said as being either unreliable or not correct, if you can't say that, then I suppose you would have to accept for the possibility that what he says may be -- may be correct. And then you would have to look at all of the other evidence in the case in deciding on the genuineness of the documents but the Prosecution -- you can never get away from that particular problem, any Prosecution can never get away from that particular problem, and the Prosecution's submission is, however, that you've got to look at all of the handwriting evidence together, in its entirety, and you can, when you do that, reject the evidence of -- you're entitled to reject his evidence. You're perfectly entitled to do that and you're entitled to reject it either as not reliable enough for you to rely upon it, or, as simply incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put this to you because apart from this aspect that I have just mentioned, there is also some -- there are also some documents that have been examined by both Mr. Fagel and Mr. Kerzan, two that you have more or less put on the same level, and they disagree amongst themselves as well. Documents that Mr. Fagel said, plus plus, Mr. Kerzan says one plus or even zero or neutral. And vice versa. MR. DI FAZIO: It's significant though that where Dr. Kerzan differs from Fagel he differs only that he couldn't come to any particular conclusion. And there, it's a fundamental difference from Professor Bilic, who in those particular cases was emphatic this is not the signature of Naser Oric. And one would have thought that in those circumstances, that Dr. Kerzan would have been able to, if indeed those signatures do display features that clearly point to them not being the signatures of Naser Oric, that he too would have reached that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me not interrupt you any further. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, just returning to Fejzic, if I might just pause there, will you permit to have a think about what Your Honours have raised and if necessary I might revisit this issue for about four or five minutes on Friday and if -- so that I can gather my thoughts about it. It's a good point and the Prosecution is not trying to evade it. I'll have -- perhaps return to you on this very briefly on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting that you were trying to avoid, Mr. Di Fazio. In fact, you will have every opportunity -- not just you but the Defence, of course, to elaborate on any argument that you need to. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. The other issue concerning Fejzic's signatures is this: You can see from annex -- what -- annex B, that the results of his -- the results of Professor Bilic's conclusions most probably not by -- sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment? Yes. In relation to P74, P73, and P75, not by Hamdija Fejzic. Those signatures were never provided, the known signatures were never provided. The Prosecution has addressed you in its closing brief, final brief, on this, at paragraph 43. We comment that it's extraordinary that an expert report relying on a number of supposed non-contentious documents as the touchstone for analysing disputed documents does not include those very signatures. It's, in the Prosecution's submission, the failure to provide those known signatures is really very damaging to the evidence of Professor Bilic. The Defence reply is also inadequate. Paragraph 106, they make the submission that it was not the decision of Professor Bilic but that of counsel. The point the Prosecution makes is that that's just beside the point. Regardless of whose decision it was, the fact is that the controls, the nine signatures, were not made available to you and that must have a devastating effect on the evidence of Bilic. It essentially it means that the tool for testing his evidence, namely cross-examination, was emasculated, so to speak. You can't do it. You can't test it in cross-examination unless you've got the known signatures. If Your Honours please, that completes my submissions on the documentation. As I said I may return to it briefly on Friday. Just to address you on this other issue that Your Honours raised this morning. But if I do, I shan't be long. I want to turn now, if Your Honours please, to the attacks, one aspect of the attacks. The Prosecution submission is that there is evidence for -- in all of the attacks of soldiers or fighters participating in the burning of villages. I don't propose to go through all of that evidence and recapitulate, sorry, restate it all. It's contained in the Prosecution brief. The Defence, in its closing brief, at paragraphs 1420 to 1424 dealt with the topic of the impossibility of dealing with civilians at the attack sites. And they were essentially, as I understand it, two defence submissions. Firstly, it's well known that the destruction was caused by civilians, and I understand that to be a reference of destruction by fire. It was caused by civilians. I'm not ignoring the other Defence theories, of course, but -- of Serb counterattack, aerial bombing, and so on, but, as I understand it, one of the more significant -- or a significant factor in the causation of the burning, who caused it, was the civilians. And the second is that they were impossible to control. The Prosecution submission is that far from being impossible to control, the -- both soldiers and civilians burnt at the villages, at the attack sites. When they did so, command responsibility attaches to the soldiers who burnt. If those soldiers at the attack sites aided and abetted the civilians in the burning of dwellings and structures, then responsibility also attaches and that's been dealt with in the Prosecution brief at length. I don't intend to go through the law or recapitulate that. It's all been set out. It's fair to say that the Defence ought to paint a picture of milling and desperate and uncoordinated and uncontrolled civilians who were gathering around in large numbers, and the reason for that is clear. It's firstly to attribute some or all of the destruction solely to civilians, and to -- furthermore to establish that any soldiers who were there were not aiding and abetting the acts of destruction carried out by civilians. Aiding and abetting, as Your Honours can see from the Prosecution final brief, paragraph 203 consists of assisting, encouraging, lending moral support to the perpetration of a crime so that it has substantial effect with the knowledge that the conduct will assist. There is on the Prosecution case a clear policy or pattern of burning that emerges from the -- from the evidence in the case. It was an ongoing activity spread over a period of time. The Prosecution final brief has addressed you at length about -- on that issue. You can recall the evidence of Pyers Tucker on the Serb concerns over the issue of the burning of villages and how that concern sharpened beyond what were their normal concerns in late 1992 and early 1993. And in the discussion on generalised evidence of burning, there is also reference to other Serb documents that clearly show a Serb preoccupation with the practice of the burning of villages in the area. So this undermines any suggestion that the burning was the spontaneous result of uncontrolled civilians and rather points to the phenomenon as being far from that. There is clear evidence in the case that at the time of the attacks in -- on the various villages, both civilians and soldiers burnt together. On the same occasions, often in close company with each other. I know what all the Defence arguments concerning lack of uniforms and the inability to distinguish. On the other hand the Prosecution submits to you that the evidence of the witnesses, when they described fighters, is generally pretty reliable. They were able to -- they felt happy in their own minds. They were able to see if people were armed, wearing camouflage uniforms or parts of camouflage uniforms, and in the Prosecution's submission, that's there for you to decide and there is nothing further that I want to add to it. But the fact that they were both engaged in burning in the same location at the same time in the Prosecution's submission is evidence of the soldiers aiding and abetting the civilians in the act of burning or torching the villages. To return to that issue of the civilians acting or cooperating with the soldiers, I just want to look at some aspects of the attacks. Firstly the attacks were, on the Prosecution case, surprise attacks. Just give me a moment, please. Yes. They were surprise attacks. The element of surprise in this situation was absolutely crucial, and it was particularly so in the case of Poljandt [phoen], attackers such as the Muslim fighting forces in this case where they were advancing into what on the Defence case are heavily fortified military compounds or villages. That element of surprise would have been utterly, totally crucial for the successful outcome of any such attack. And that's why there is evidence of a number of the attacks at least occurring at dawn or thereabouts. And it was imperative therefore that in order to preserve that civilians needed to cooperate with the soldiers and vice versa. The civilians knew their role at the start of the attack. The fact of convergence of civilians at attack sites also indicates a degree of working together. The Defence case, of course, is that everyone knew the attacks, the attack site, and they couldn't be stopped from gathering. The Prosecution submission is that that is simply not so, in the evidential scenario in this case. It was a matter of life or death. Success or failure of an attack was a matter of life or death. It was imperative that the element of surprise be maintained and is imperative therefore that the civilians have to have had some sort of understanding of their role at the attack sites. And Kada Hotic -- excuse me. Kara Hotic, who testified on behalf of the Defence, demonstrated how easy it was to simply keep the civilians away. That was the idea. She was talking about letter son, who was a -- who would go off to fight. She said, "I didn't know what time the fighters would leave. I didn't see that and I couldn't always know something like that. Even when my son was leaving the house, sometimes he would go to his friends and he wouldn't even say anything to me. He wouldn't say goodbye. This happened also." That's at 9809. That's a simple demonstration, if Your Honours please, of how, if fighters wanted to keep the attack site quiet, concealed, from other civilians, it was possible to do so, and it's even more imperative if the element of surprise is one of the crucial factors in your ability to successfully carry out an attack as it must have been in this case with Muslim fighters who were probably not as well armed as the Serbs on the Defence case. The civilians also knew what to do at the attack sites. Kada Hotic also testified about that need to keep quiet at the attack sites and she said, "Everyone was aware that they had to be quiet so that they wouldn't be noticed." That's at 9810. And at 9815 of the transcript she said there was a kind of implicit agreement. And this is a picture that's at complete variance with the Defence case of uncontrolled melee there. So there is clear evidence of the civilians and the fighters having some sort of working understanding. There is also evidence that the attacks were committed to obtain food as well as other strictly more military objectives, and it is the Prosecution's submission that they, the civilians, had to play a vital role in that. It was imperative that they obtain as much food as quickly and as fast -- as quickly and as comprehensively as they could in order for these attacks to be carried out successfully, particularly so where the food gathering is the main object of the attack. P84 contains references to the envisaged obtaining of large quantities of food. Sorry, would Your Honours just give me a moment? There are references in P84 to I think at page 4 of P84 there is a reference to the need to set up a warehouse and a reference to smuggling, the need to stop smuggling of food. And in the context of what we all know about what was going on at the time in 1992, that reference to smuggling in P84, in the Prosecution's submission, can only be a reference, reasonable reference, to stopping solo civilians taking away food, food for themselves, and it does n the Prosecution's submission, tend to indicate something level of organisation for the civilians. In those circumstances, in all of those circumstances, in the Prosecution submission, given the pattern of burning, the level of cooperation and working together, the Prosecution's submission is that where the civilians conducted burning, the fighters or soldiers must have been aiding and abetting them. Thank you, Your Honours. That now completes my submissions on the attacks. As I said, I'll return briefly to address you on the issue of hostile witnesses. So my colleagues will now address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Di Fazio. Who is next? Ms. Richardson or Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you return to me. Just give me one second so I can move the lectern. Your Honours, Mr. Di Fazio has already started our review of the crime base. He looked at the attack sites. He raised a couple of points, emphasised those that we have already briefed you in our closing brief. But to further explain, I will now do that with what we refer to as the first prison scenario and then Ms. Richardson will do that with the second prison scenario. You have heard the evidence, in particular, of Nedeljko Radic and Mr. Zikic, two men who were imprisoned in the Srebrenica SUP building. Nedeljko Radic comes around September 15th whereas Mr. Zikic comes after the attack on Fakovici, the 5th of October. I would like to highlight a bit of the evidence that leads you to questions of subordination, modes of liability, and identification. In respect to the attack at Podravanje that incorporated the capture of Nedeljko Radic at the mine in Branka on the 25th of September, and then also Mr. Dragutin Kukic, who dies in the first prison scenario, along with the imprisonment of Bubanj, Saric, and the men in that very first instance, I think the Trial Chamber should be reminded that the Defence has often said they were beaten before they got to the prison. And this is true. They did arrive at the prison in a state where their bodies had suffered physical blows. And the only evidence related to those physical blows is that they were inflicted on numerous occasions by subordinates of Zulfo Tursunovic. Naser Oric's subordinates have already beaten those prisoners prior to them arriving at the SUP. Zulfo Tursunovic is aware that it's his men who had to take Nedeljko Radic in particular to his house and then they received word that they could be transported to the prison in Srebrenica. Mr. Radic arrives in his underwear. His clothes have been taken, which is not an unusual practice according to the Defence theory, that at times clothes were taken from members of the enemy, often from dead bodies. When Nedeljko Radic arrives in his underwear, it's uncertain how many days that he was in his underwear before Cude a military police officer who was a guard at the prison, admitted to by the Defence, gives his a blanket. I highlight this point because it has often been raised that the beatings left wounds and injuries only on the body and not on the face. Therefore, Naser Oric, if he were at the prison, and it's certainly the Prosecution's position that he was at the prison, couldn't see any of the injuries. Well, Cude gave a blanket to Nedeljko Radic but it's uncertain and quite possible that the body of Nedeljko Radic, at times his legs and his chest, were visible. Your Honours, the beatings that the men received during the first prison scenario are beatings that the military police not only had knowledge of, were aware of. They also assisted. Now, we go back to that issue that we've raised many times, where the military police, the guards at the prison. We've already spoken again about Cude, Sabahudin Omerovic, listed as a military police officer. If we go to the transcript of Nedeljko Radic at 3528 or 3613, more evidence of police officers, whether they are giving guards, giving order to the prisoners or they are functioning as guards. Now, one has to say, and the Defence is certainly accepted, that Cude was the good guard. What made him the good guard? He didn't allow people to come into the cell to beat the prisoners. He knew that was incorrect. But Cude did open up the cell and allow the prisoners to go out, at times one by one, to be beaten by Kemo and Mrki. Was Cude afraid of Kemo, afraid of Mrki, or was this where the one time his good conscious necessary was not in effect? The Prosecution does not in any way try to speculate about motive but by opening the door to the cell, and allowing the men to be beaten, sequentially, he has facilitated those beatings. He has assisted those beatings, perhaps unwillingly, perhaps regrettably, but he has aided and abetted in the beatings of the prisoners in the very least by Kemo and by Mrki. We have other information too, when the turnkey is present. It's present when Kemo urinates into the mouth of Nedeljko Radic and Mrki is present also. This reference to be 3691 until 3692. In the very least, Cude knew the difference, he knew that he could prevent and he knew what it meant not to prevent the beatings. Another matter that the Trial Chamber should consider, and this goes to several issues but in particular inquiry notice of Mr. Oric during the first prison period, is that his deputy, Akif Ustic, came to the prison. This is at the transcript 3623. Akif Ustic comes to the prison, once again we have a military presence at the prison, and he assures the prisoners, "We will treat new regard to the Geneva Conventions." Now it's not the Prosecution's position that Akif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, or Naser Oric knew every provision of the 4th Geneva Convention in regard to civilians or the 3rd in regard to prisoners of war. But they certainly knew that there were legal safeguards that they were to respect in regard to detaining prisoners of war and civilians. And they assured the prisoners, Akif Ustic assures the prisoners, "We will treat you with regard to the Geneva Conventions." Between Zulfo Tursunovic and Akif Ustic, Naser Oric is certainly aware that there are prisoners and that there are duties in regard to the prison, these prisoners. The Trial Chamber should not overlook the significance of this evidence. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber should understand that the visitors to the prison do not include the civilian war president. Hajrudin Avdic did not come to the prison. Mr. Bogilovic does not come to the prison, nor his deputy Nurija Jusufovic. This is not the matter of a civilian authorities. Now, the Defence would want us to believe that because there were 11 prisoners, really Serb citizens, detained from Karno in the month of August, and for that we have a handwritten note to Avdic, first name Avdic, saying, "People are detained. What should I do with them?" They would want that one-time experience of finding a link between persons involved in the War Presidency to be proof that the War Presidency had the responsibility for the prisoners or in the very least the responsibility of Mirzet Halilovic who they know had responsibility for the prisoners. The evidence is not only not convincing. There is a bit of illogic. There is certainly no follow-up. Why didn't any members of the Presidency come to the prison or arrange the exchange, even the first one that failed, talking on the radio. Naser Oric did that with the prisoner Sadic. It wasn't even the liaison person. Hamdija Fejzic didn't exercise his executive role there to be the link between the military and the War Presidency in regard to the prisoners. The prisoners' affair was a military affair. Detained, processed, and exchanged, and guarded. These were the affairs of the Srebrenica armed forces. The timing is crucial. The Defence attempted to have Mr. Bogilovic state that it was really the military police who were the subordinates to the civilians and on cross-examination -- and right now I'm referring to transcript page 6430. But Mr. Bogilovic could not agree with them that the military police came under the War Presidency prior to his having a special supervisory relationship to Mirzet Halilovic. So from the moment that the prisoners were picked up September 25th, October 5th, we are talking about the responsibility of the Srebrenica armed forces commanded by Naser Oric. The War Presidency had no responsibility, doesn't appear that they had any administrative tasking in regard to the prisoners. The Defence theory of Karno shows that there were civilians that were detained and sometimes the War Presidency involved themselves in it. It can show nothing more than that. The only other time that we have a civilian presence near the prisons is Zeli [phoen], who happened to stop by a stretcher. But that will be addressed in the second prison scenario. The exchange of prisoners is important. It's vital. It's the ability to get fighting men back and regrettably dead soldiers back. I believe that there were officers, Lieutenant Rex Dudley and the CanBat officers, who talked about the question of morale that was involved in knowing that if you fell during battle on the enemy line, that your body would be brought home to bury, and I think that that was taken very seriously, and as a result, the matter of prisoners is very serious because that is what we use for exchange. After Akif Ustic is killed, immediately, immediately, the prisoners will be exchanged. That is the next subject that I'd like to talk about, issues and evidence around that exchange. Because the Defence has now thrown a theory of the Naser Oric look alike, Mrki, being present on the night prior to the prison exchange. They would have Your Honours consider that it was Mrki who asked the prisoners about Akif Ustic, conceding that Mrki Omerovic was a member of Akif Ustic's unit and therefore had emotional ties and was extremely upset at the death of Akif Ustic. If he was a member of the unit then that places him within the Stari Grad unit that's based in Srebrenica, places him as a subordinate from the very beginning, under Naser Oric. But the theory of Mrki being present in the room that night doesn't hold. It's because Nedeljko Radic, who at this point in time, has been beaten several nights by Kemo and by Mrki, he recognised who Mrki is and who is not Mrki. He was able to come back to us the day after his first day of giving evidence in court and correct himself and say, well, Mrki had the uniform. He had a uniform on, as a matter of fact, that looked like Naser Oric's because it had lilies on it. He never once said, and Mrki himself looks like Naser Oric. Spoke about them as two separate individuals. Nedeljko Radic wasn't certain whether Mrki was in the room the night that Naser Oric asked the prisoners, don't you know about Akif Ustic? The reason he wasn't certain could only assist Your Honours in understanding that he was certain that Naser Oric was not Mrki. Now, one could say Naser Oric came to the first prison and identified himself, "I'm Naser Oric." The Defence would have you believe that's Mrki fooling around again, making us laugh, that's a joke. That can't be true. The evidence shows that when Naser Oric came into the SUP building there was a hush that came about. One would think that when Mrki walked into the SUP building people were ready for a joke. There would be no lowering of the volume of the hush because the commander was there. It was Naser Oric who walked into the prison, into the cells. The Defence theory of Mrki is one of those double knots that they've tied a little too tight at the end. Not only it doesn't make sense, it points in the opposite direction. We have prisoners who know Naser Oric. Sadic knew him from before the war, is taken out of the cell, conducts the radio calls to the Serb authorities related to the exchange. Nedeljko Radic, who Sadic informs "that's Naser Oric." But after the first time that Nedeljko Radic and the other prisoners see Naser Oric then they recognise him and the subsequent times they see him, in particular when they are taken out of the room on the night before the exchange. Zikic sees Naser Oric, they speak, might be a little confused about when and whom Naser Oric relates the Arkan story - excuse me - about when and whom Arkan marries his wife, such a big event but he knows that Arkan married a famous singer. When he came to testify here he confused those facts. I don't think that Naser Oric told Mr. Zikic at that point in time anything about the marriage of Arkan. I think he was talking about the gun that he had. I think he was talking about that ambush that made him famous. And I don't think that Mr. Zikic forgets that conversation or with whom he had it. From that point on, if he didn't know Naser Oric, he certainly knew him and recognised him. Nedeljko Radic sees Naser Oric afterwards, states that he's 100 per cent sure, sees Naser Oric in a film on a horse, and then recognises him again when he's brought to The Hague. Now, the Defence tried to shake that recognition. Mr. Nedeljko listened a bit amused, but if you grow a beard, if you put on weight, if I know you I know you, I recognise you. It doesn't mean someone can't change. We have three very good instances of recognition, identity, in the first prison scene. We have confirmation Naser Oric wears a uniform, that his deputy comes to the prison and that his future deputy, Zulfo Tursunovic, his subordinates actually escort the prisoners. The guards have aided and abetted the physical beatings. The Defence then tries to run to what appears to be almost another theory. Well, Mirzet Halilovic was punished. There was no failure to punish. He was removed. They say "I reported him to the War Presidency," still trying to make Your Honours embellish the War Presidency as having responsibility. Well, let's assume that part of what they are saying is true. Let's assume that Naser Oric exercised his duty to punish Mirzet Halilovic, even under, let's say, a joint command theory. Shows he's capable, shows he can act, shows that it is a horrible thing to maltreat, mistreat prisoners, particularly to kill prisoners. This should be more than sufficient evidence to Your Honours that Naser Oric can act, does have effective control, when he chooses to exercise it, and more importantly, that act of dismissing Mirzet Halilovic should put him on inquiry notice about the prison, because something doesn't make sense. Now, the Prosecution committed a grammatical error in the closing brief. We forgot a period. We might have misled the Trial Chamber and, with regrets to the Defence, of ever suggesting that Naser Oric was in the room in the cell when the body of Kukic was in the cell. There should have been a period that said Kukic's body was there until 10.00 in the morning, period, when Naser Oric came. Naser Oric came at a different time. The body wasn't there. The body was gone, disappeared, missing. He asked about Mr. Kukic and he's informed quite hesitantly that he died of a heart attack. Why didn't he ask where was the body? I can still exchange that. That suffices for me to receive bodies back of my men back in return. Is the body buried in the church cemetery where other prisoners was buried? Was the body taken to the hospital? The body disappeared. Is this the person that Mirzet Halilovic beat to death? Were the prisoners not telling me the truth? It wasn't a hard attack? Oh, this is the person Mirzet killed? Should I ask Cude? One of the guards? Anyone else? He said he'd leave it up to the military court. That was their job. Oh, so was there a functioning entity of some type who was supposed to look into that, that was military-based, and did they? No. Naser Oric was able to punish. He failed to follow up because the real information that he could have uncovered were the nightly beatings by Mrki, Kemo, and the killing of Dragutin Kukic by Kemo. He doesn't do that. The last time he comes to the prison it's because of Akif Ustic. And, Your Honours, I would like for you to look at small video again from the prison, and whereas before, the Trial Chamber looked at the video in regard to corroborating the evidence of Nedeljko Radic, corroborating recognition by Mr. Saric of Naser Oric. I would ask you to look at it again for a very different reason. And this is P448, if you give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has shown this video this time because this video is evidence of Naser Oric failing to prevent. The night before the prisoners are exchanged, he sees that the prisoners are bloodied. He himself is mad because his deputy has been killed. What he asked Mr. Saric is, "What happened to you?" There might even be a question of, was this question asked the following day. But let's say we are still in the room on the night before the exchange even though it appears to be a past tense conversation, "What happened to you?" He says, "I never hit a prisoner before. You know I hit you." Seems to be a past tense conversation. "You know I hit you and I never hit a prisoner." Naser Oric knows the difference between how one is supposed to treat prisoners and how one is not supposed to treat prisoners. Mr. Saric once again does what many people in powerless positions do in front of authority, when they know that they have done something wrong, they will say, Oh, I hit the door on the way out. But Your Honours have to understand that in the room that night is the presence of, in the very least, Kemo, the well-known, extremely violent Kemo. The next day, who is given the task, the responsibility, to drive the prisoners to the exchange going to Potocari? It's not the War Presidency. It's Kemo. Kemo, who has just seen his superior commander hit a prisoner, who has seen the prisoners bloodied. It's he who is given the task to deal with the prisoners the next day. And so what happens on the day of the exchange? Prisoners are taken out of the cell, two of the prisoners make it to the truck, and that's Nedeljko Radic and Mr. Zikic. The other two prisoners, Nevenko and Branko don't quite make it to the truck prior to being taken off again. The Defence would have us believe it was after they left the SUP but if we just look at the transcript at 3617 through 18 we'll see that they were taken back into the SUP where Kemo was, and that's where the Defence admits they probably received one of their worst beatings, probably one of their worst beatings. And the next day we have one of those prisoners who succumbs to their injuries. It's not part of our indictment. We are only talking about the cruel treatment that inflected upon them. And we have the visible injuries to Mr. Saric who the Defence says maybe that happened on the day of the exchange. We are still in the SUP, in the confines of the military part of the police. We have Kemo, notorious, with these prisoners, and Naser Oric who saw them the night before, know that is they have been beaten even warns Mr. Saric, "Don't tell them I beat you. You know I only hit you once." Did not turn to Kemo, did not say anything about, "I don't want anyone to touch these prisoners until they get to where they are going, until they are exchanged." He failed to prevent. So, Your Honour, our worst case scenario, the first prison scene, involves not just failure to investigate, further punish, punish Mirzet Halilovic, but failure to prevent. The Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt the cruel treatment, the death, superior authority, the criminal acts of subordinates, be they in a direct chain of command, such as Kemo, aiding and abetting by the guards. In essence we would submit to you we have proven beyond a reasonable doubt counts 1 and 2 as they relate to the prison scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While you're still on counts 1 and 2, you would have certainly given attention to one of the submissions of the Defence in relation to Kemo, and that is that Radic, if I'm not mistaken, repeatedly refers not to Kemo Mehmedovic but to Kemo Ahmetovic. And this has been made an issue by the Defence in their final brief. Do you have any submissions on this regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would emphasise our submissions that we placed in our reply. Mr. Radic did not know Kemo the person. He should have said Kemo Mehmedovic. He said Kemo Ahmetovic but he most often called him by the name that most people called him, Kemo from Pale. As a matter of fact, Kemo from Pale was so notorious that, like Madonna, he was just referred to as Kemo from Pale. Everyone knew who that was. Now, if -- if Mr. Radic had wanted to be less than truthful he would have come here and said Kemo Mehmedovic I said that let me straighten this up. He didn't know the last name. He wasn't from that area. And there are situations when people are more known by their nickname than by their actual name. I think technically, the Defence has raised the issue as to the correct last name of Kemo. I do not think that the Defence has raised or can succeed on its claim that Kemo from Pale was the person or was not the person who beat the prisoners or killed Mr. Kukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the point made by the Defence in their brief was that during Radic's testimony, the possibility of him being mistaken about the surname of Kemo was put to him and he repeatedly kept his position that the Kemo that was there was not -- was Kemo Ahmetovic. In other words, he never said - this is the submission of the Defence, obviously I'm not commenting upon it, I'm just asking you to comment - he never said, "Could be, it was Mehmedovic. I don't know. I didn't know the man well. I may be mistaken in the name." When this was posited to him he said, "No, it's Kemo Ahmetovic and I stick to that." And he stuck to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and he stuck to his mistake. He didn't try to change it but he knew he was speaking about Kemo from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your submission. Okay. Who is next now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Next Ms. Richardson will talk about the second prison scenario.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this morning I will conduct the Prosecution's submission on the prison scenario. We call it the second prison scenario, as it happened in the early part of January 1993 towards -- sometime after March. And it's a scenario that also deals with the counts of murder and cruel treatment. I will not rehash to Your Honours the testimony of the witnesses who were here and testified extensively about the treatment they received in the prison. I will just briefly go over some points that I think that the Trial Chamber may find helpful to be reminded of. And the first submission that the Prosecution at this moment would make to the Trial Chamber is that based on all of the evidence of the witnesses, including the survivors, the male prisoners who survived the prison ordeal in Srebrenica in 1993 and the female prisoners, that the Prosecution proved beyond a reasonable doubt that murder and cruel treatment did in fact occur in the police station, as well as the building behind the municipal building that we commonly -- we have referred to quite frequently in the Prosecution's case as the prison. These beatings, Your Honour, were committed by the guards of the prison as well as soldiers identified by witnesses who were familiar with certain individuals as soldiers, as well as by other individuals who were permitted to enter both the police station as well as the prison to what we consider a brutal and savage beatings of the male prisoners and as a result a number of them died in the prison. And I will go over that shortly. I would first like to discuss with you the first prison scenario -- sorry, the police station in the second prison scenario, and recount for you the testimony of Ilija Ivanovic who testified about being beaten at the police station. And our Prosecution final brief deals with this in paragraphs 412 as well as other areas and you may revisit it in the transcript, 4004. And, of course, you may recall that Mr. Ivanovic was here for some time and he testified extensively about the beatings he received, the injuries that he received, some of which were permanent, and he told Your Honours that he had been initiated into the police station by being kicked, literally, in his back, into the cell where he banged his head against a radiator rendering him unconscious. And you may recall that he testified that when he arrived, Kostadin Popovic, Ratko Nikolic, Milosav Milovanovic, aka Miko from Sase, Bogdan, and later Mile Trifunovic also arrived. It's our submission, Your Honour, that all of the prisoners were beaten based on his testimony and the testimony of Ratko Nikolic. They were beaten during the time that they spent in the police station, and as my colleague, Ms. Sellers, mentioned, it's the Prosecution's position that the prisoners were under the prisoners were guarded by military police, Your Honour, and I believe that a number of the document that is the Prosecution has put forward bear that out. In addition to the patrol reports, Prosecution Exhibit 16, the military police log, which lists and details the Serb prisoners that were brought in, and logged the information, personal details, et cetera. You may recall a number of the witnesses verified the personal information that was found in both the military log and other documents. Some of those documents were, we believe, the product of the security organ headed by Hamed Salihovic. I would also remind Your Honours of the testimony of 007, who testified that he had arrived in Srebrenica from Cerska in the company of Dragan Ilic, Jakov Dokic, Ande Radic [phoen], and Branko Sekulic came later on. The Prosecution dealt with the documents which verified this information, verified they were brought in by soldiers, and confirm and corroborates our position that it was the military police based on their patrol reports as well as the -- the military police log that they were in charge of the prisoners. Naser Oric himself, during his interview, testified that Hamed -- not testified, excuse me, but stated to our investigators that Hamed Salihovic was charged with interrogating the prisoners and taking notes from them, and the fact that the military police were in charge of the prisoners. So there is no doubt, Your Honour, based on the evidence presented during the Prosecution's case that the guards were the military police at the police station. You may also recall that the witnesses testified, both the females, witnesses, Stana Stamenic, Milena Mitrovic, and the male prisoners, Ande Radic as well, that after being detained at the military police station they were then transferred to the prison. Your Honour, these beatings continued at the prison. It's our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. submission that the guards at the prison, as well as soldiers, were responsible for the beatings, and I will address that in a moment, but there is no doubt, and I believe that the testimony of the witnesses as well as the medical documentation, proved beyond a reasonable doubt that they were in fact brutally beaten to the point at which Kostadin Popovic died, Milisav Milanovic died, Dragan Ilic died, Branko Sekulic died, and we also submit that Jakov Dokic died. You may recall that Ratko Nikolic testified at length about being beaten and you can refer to his testimony in the Prosecution's final brief at paragraph 420. You may recall that he testified that the prisoners were brought out of the cell one by one and beaten, not as the Defence would like to suggest that these beatings took place in this dark cell where they were unable to identify who beat them. Ilija Ivanovic also confirmed to you that he was taken out to the reception area and I will deal with that shortly whether we get to the issue of identification. I would just like to segue for a moment to the identification of the individuals doing the beatings. Ilija Ivanovic testified that he was beaten by Dzemo Tihic who he believed was a soldier, and the Prosecution would like to point out -- at least highlight one clarification with respect to what was stated in the Prosecution's final brief regarding Mr. Ilija Ivanovic's identification of Dzemo Tihic as the person who beat him. The Prosecution in fact stated in paragraph 416 that Dzemo Tihic broke the cheek bone of Ilija Ivanovic, which is what Mr. Ivanovic testified to. But then there was an error made because we later stated in 436 that it was Ahmo Tihic. However, just looking at those two paragraphs, Your Honour, it was clear that there was a mistake in the name. The information is exactly the same. And we stand by what Mr. Ilija Ivanovic said in paragraph 416, that it was Dzemo Tihic who he knew prior to the war that broke his cheek bone. Mr. Ivanovic also testified that the people who were beating the prisoners wore camouflage uniforms and civilian clothing and the combination. And we believe, Your Honour, that this description of the guards, also corroborated by Branimir Mitrovic who spent a substantial amount of time in the prison, who also testified that the guards he observed beating the prisoners wore both civilian and military clothing, camouflage uniforms, Stana Mitrovic, Stana Stamanovic [phoen] testified that it was the soldiers who wore camouflage -- that the guards were wearing camouflage uniform as well. Your Honour, I submit to you that you should not be distracted by the description of the guards and be wedded to what they were wearing to make a determination as to who the guards were and whether they were in fact beating the prisoners. The Prosecution submits that the guards wore camouflage uniform and civilian uniform, and as a result, Your Honour, some of the witnesses may have been confused by the fact that they were beaten by someone wearing civilian uniform and may not have equated that person with being -- either being a soldier or a guard, and that they may have somehow deduced that the civilian clothing meant that it was a civilian beating them, and we would suggest to Your Honours that that is not the issue. The issue is that they were beaten by the guards who wore both civilian and camouflage uniform and that is what Your Honour should consider as determining who did the actual beating. It's our position again that the guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't quite follow the argument, to be honest with you because you are suggesting that we shouldn't allow ourselves to be misguided this uniform aspect. At the same time you are using the uniform aspect and Mitrovic's testimony precisely to indicate that the guards were, at least when they were wearing a uniform, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The onus of proof lies with you. It's not a question of suggesting this or suggesting that. What you have to prove --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can restate the argument, Your Honour. My point referring to the testimony of Stana Stamenic was the fact that there were a variety of description of the clothing worn by the guards. And so if one witness stated that you -- that testified before Your Honours that civilian clothing worn by someone who beat him, that that person may have concluded that this was a civilian, should not determine the issue, Your Honour, and that the issue should be doesn't matter what the individuals were wearing, because we have heard a variety of descriptions, worn by the guards that what in fact Your Honour should consider is the testimony of individuals who stated that it was the guards who beat them and not necessarily link the clothing to the -- link the clothing to determine whether or not the beatings were conducted by guards or civilians. I don't know if I'm clear on that and I can say it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I can understand what you're saying but Judge Eser wore like to have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just with regard to the issue of uniforms, you spoke of camouflage uniforms, civilian uniform, and civilian clothing. Now, when you speak of civilian uniform, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I stated civilian uniform, Your Honour, I misspoke. It's civilian clothing. Indeed, the witnesses stated that the guards wore camouflage uniforms, civilian clothing, and sometimes it was a mixed combination. And my submission is that if a witness stated that it was -- that they were beaten by someone wearing civilian clothing, that Your Honours not consider that as determining or concluding that it was a civilian who beat the prisoners. It is our submission that the guards wore a combination of clothing. Your Honour, I'm being told that it may be close to a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. Let's have a break now. Do you prefer 25- or a 30-minute break, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: A 30-minute break would be better, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 30-minute break and take it up from there. After you, who will take it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Richardson will take the next session, and then I will state and then Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you anticipate you will finish today? MR. DI FAZIO: Easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see it that way. All right. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I with would just like the record to reflect that we are joined by co-counsel Jose Doria this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, Your Honour, I believe the Prosecution were on the submissions that the guards who were the ones beating the prisoners in the prison, as testified to by Ilija Ivanovic, Branko Mitrovic who said he saw them beat Mr. Ivanovic and others in the hallway and that the guards were wearing a -- mixed clothing, sometimes they had uniforms, sometimes they wore civilian clothing. It's our submission, Your Honour, that the guards were the military police, just a continuation of their responsibilities from the first prison scenario, this time under Akif Kurcic [phoen] whom the Prosecution referred to in their brief, and I believe we have pointed to the documentation which supports his appointment by the Srebrenica armed forces. Your Honour, Mr. Ratko Nikolic -- as we move to an aspect of the prison which involves the murders of five prisoners, you may recall Mr. Ratko Nikolic testified that he remembers Kostadin Popovic dying, he remembers that Kostadin Popovic's body was taken away but before it was taken away it was wrapped in a blanket, a note was put in with his name and information, and then that this body was taken away. The Defence would have you believe that this is not correct and that Mr. Kostadin Popovic's body was never actually in fact recovered as they sought to challenge the credibility of Dr. Stankovic's report and the identification of Mr. Kostadin Popovic's body by his son, Nikola Popovic. The Prosecution submits that the testimony of Nikola Popovic, that he identified his father's body, that in fact there was a note with the information that it was the clothing he was wearing when he was captured as well as the gold tooth that we all heard so much about during the cross-examination was what led him to believe that that was his father. If the Court examines Dr. Popovic's autopsy report that deals specifically with the autopsy of Kostadin Popovic, the Court will see what the Prosecution submits based on a series of pictures is a note that is referred to in the autopsy report itself with the information as testified to by Kostadin Popovic. And as the Court examines the pictures that are attached to Dr. Stankovic's report, the Prosecution invites the Court to examine the pictures very carefully as the Court may -- well, the Prosecution believe -- may observe is a note that was taken a picture of. Of course, you can not read it but clearly there is a piece of paper there that is attached to the report as part what was recovered on the body of Nikola -- of Vladko Sinin Popovic [phoen]. Your Honour, the death of Dragan Ilic, the Defence would have you believe that there is not such evidence to support his death. However, the Prosecution would refer Your Honours to the testimony of 007 -- of confidential witness 007 who testified that Dragan Ilic died, Your Honour, as he was laying next to him following a beating. The Prosecution submits that this is more than sufficient evidence of the death of Dragan Ilic and that no further corroboration is needed as suggested by the Defence. The death of Milisav Milovanovic, the Prosecution also addressed in paragraph 86 of the Prosecution's reply brief, as well as in the Prosecution's final brief, as well as Ilija Ivanovic testified to his death, transcript 4074, and you should also be referred to the transcript of C-0007 at 4636. There is no doubt that Milisav Milovanovic is the Mico referred to in the Prosecution's indictment as well as in documents from the Srebrenica -- that came out of Srebrenica which refers to the prisoners, although the Defence would have the Trial Chamber believe that there was no identification of Mico, the Prosecution submit that there was substantial identification of Mico as Milisav Milovanovic by Ilija Ivanovic. Your Honour, the death of Branko Sekulic was also addressed by the Prosecution in its final brief and we refer you to paragraph 440 to 441 dealing with the evidence of his death. Now, I would like to turn to the next Serb victim for which the Prosecution alleged murder occurred in the prison of the Srebrenica -- in the prison in Srebrenica in 1993, and that is Jakov Dokic. The Defence would have Your Honours believe that since Jakov Dokic was last seen alive by 007 in the prison in Srebrenica that in fact the Prosecution has not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Jakov Dokic died in Srebrenica prison. It's the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, that based on all of the evidence the death of Jakov Dokic was proved circumstantially, and I would refer you to documents which support the fact that he was brought into the prison, Prosecution Exhibit 16 which details Jakov Dokic being brought in from Cerska with other prisoners such as Dragan Ilic, Brado Pajic [phoen], Ande Radic. And witnesses testified that Mr. Dokic was imprisoned with them and these witnesses were Ilija Ivanovic as well as Ande Radic, and I would refer to you Prosecution final brief 436 and 442. Prosecution Exhibit 45 also lists Mr. Dokic as one of the prisoners that was imprisoned in Srebrenica along with Kostadin Popovic, and if we could just take a look at that exhibit, which is now in Sanction, as you can see Mr. Dokic is listed as the first individual and this document is dated the 9th of February 1993. Towards the end you see the names of Kostadin Popovic and Bogdan Zivanovic and it is alleged that these individuals were already deceased and that the bodies of these individuals as well as the above individuals were listed for being exchanged. And this was a document that the Prosecution believes was created by the committee of mediation and exchange. The Defence would have you believe that Prosecution Exhibit 19, which lists Mr. Dokic as having died, if we could just have that illustrated on the Sanction, that this document does not support -- or does not provide proof that Jakov Dokic died in Srebrenica as this document also lists Rado Pejic as having died and that that was not true. I believe what Your Honour should keep in mind with respect to this document more importantly is that with the exception of Rado Pejic all the other information on this document is true. You heard from multiple witnesses about the fact that they were in prison with these individuals, you heard that they were present when certain individuals died, including Branko Sekulic as well as Dragan Ilic. That information is correct. They are listed as having died. Ratko Nikolic was captured and you heard from Ratko Nikolic yourself as well as Mile Mitrovic. I will not go through all of the names on the document, Your Honour, but suffice to say that the majority of the information is in fact true. The fact that Rado Pejic did not die, I believe, is something that the Court should take note of but should rely more importantly on the overwhelming amount of information that is true. Your Honour, the Defence would make much to do about the fact that Ilija Ivanovic said that he heard that Jakov Dokic was alive and Mr. Ivanovic never said he saw him, he never even give us any information about who he heard this from except for the off comment that he was alive and had been thrown out of Srebrenica by the defendant. I submit to Your Honours that this information was not correct, Mr. Ilija Ivanovic was, I believe, a bit confused about that and based on the testimony of the father of Jakov Dokic who said that he's -- hasn't seen his son since 1992. I submit to Your Honours that Jakov Dokic is not alive and well and living in Bosnia or any other country but in fact he succumbed to his injuries that he received in Srebrenica as a result of the brutal beating at the hands of the guards who we submit were the military police. And, Your Honour, we believe that the evidence of the deaths of the other prisoners such as Dragan Ilic and Kostadin Popovic, Milisav Milovanovic and Branko Sekulic proves, if not directly but circumstantially that Jakov Dokic as well succumbed to the injuries he received as a result of the beatings. Your Honour, this Tribunal has recognised that that can be inferred circumstantially from the evidence if the facts may unavoidably lead to this conclusion, and it's the submission of the Prosecution that the facts do -- does in fact lead to this conclusion. In the Kunarac Trial Chamber, it was held that proof of death beyond a reasonable doubt, that a person was -- murdered does not necessarily require proof that the dead body of that person had been recovered. The fact of the victim's death can be inferred circumstantially from all of the evidence presented to the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber also added, Your Honour, that a victim's death may be established by circumstantial evidence provided that the only reasonable inference is that the victim is dead as a result of the acts and the omissions of the accused. I believe, Your Honour -- the Prosecution is of the opinion, Your Honour, that this is the exact scenario we have here, that based on all of the facts of the witnesses, the brutal beatings of the prisoners, the ones that died thereafter, the fact that Mr. Dokic was still in the prison when he was last seen as confirmed by confidential witness 007, the Prosecution is of the opinion that it need not have produced the body. Our Tribunal jurisprudence does not require that. And that the Court -- that the Trial Chamber may come to a conclusion based on all the evidence that has been presented that this is the reasonable inference to be drawn. With respect to the Cerska prisoners, Your Honour, the issue of causation has also been raised with respect to the prisoners brought in from Cerska and as Your Honour recalled, the witnesses were very candid in that they had been beaten. You heard from Ande Radic -- Radovic, excuse me, who stated that the male prisoners brought in with her who had been beaten. Ivanovic also said, yes, they told him that they had been beaten. There is no doubt and the Prosecution concedes that they were not treated well in Cerska. However, Your Honour, as they were brought in Srebrenica, their beatings continued and it was a result of these beatings, Your Honour, that they died and not as a result of some opportunistic disease associated with lice or malnutrition as the Defence seems to contend. The Prosecution stands by its submission in the reply brief that in fact, Your Honour, if that were the case, the women may have also died as a result and there is no evidence of that, and it is most likely, Your Honour, that they died. A reasonable inference can be drawn, logical conclusion, and, as well, based on the direct evidence of witnesses who stated that the Cerska prisoners looked even worse following their beatings in Srebrenica. You may recall Andja Radic said she went to see the prisoners and she was surprised. She expressed that she was surprised that they looked even worse. Ilija Ivanovic said that they looked even worse and he particularly, upon being cross-examined on this issue, said, absolutely not, they did not die from the Cerska -- from the wounds received from Cerska and he refuted that suggestion placed by the Defence. I believe the Prosecution is of the opinion that these witnesses were credible, and that in fact that their deaths were caused by the beatings. In any event, Your Honour, having said that, a very fundamental principle in criminal law is that you take your victim as you find him. That principle applies to this Tribunal, Your Honour, and is reflected in our jurisprudence as well. And if the Court would refer to Prosecution versus Delalic, paragraph 909, it is -- they quote this very well-known principle. "It is a well-recognised legal principle that a wrongdoer must take the victim as he finds him. Thus if a perpetrator by his acts shortened the life of his victim it is legally relevant that the victim may have died shortly thereafter from another cause." To establish criminal liability in situations where there are pre-existing physical conditions which would cause the victim's death, therefore, it is only necessary to establish that the accused's conduct contributed to the death of the victim. Therefore, the fact, Your Honour, that the conditions in Srebrenica were appalling and that the victims may have been suffering from other complaints such as lice simply does not nullify the action on the part of the subordinates of Naser Oric. And those subordinates being the guards, soldiers and others, the guards being those of the military police. Your Honour, I believe we have covered significantly and sufficiently the cruel treatment that was meted out to the prisoners, and we stand by the evidence that was presented with respect to Stanko Mitrovic, called Cane, and that evidence was presented by Ilija Ivanovic, transcript 4068 to 4069, who testified that Stanko called Cane was beaten by the soldiers and that he was disabled and he was beaten specifically on his hands and legs. Those limbs. They would target those limbs, Your Honour. We also heard about the situation where the beard of confidential witness 007 was set on fire. You heard Mr. Ivanovic testify to that and you heard the witness himself who suffered this horrific act testify to it as well. We believe that the evidence is sufficient with respect to the cruel treatment and just briefly with respect to Milo -- Mile Trivunovic [phoen] whose granddaughter testified that she was present in the prison, had heard the screams of the prisoners and her grandfather moaning, and that she had seen her grandfather, he was black and blue, that he died shortly after being released and exchanged from the Srebrenica prison. Your Honour, we believe that this evidence is sufficient to sustain the charge of cruel treatment on behalf of those prisoners. Your Honour, with respect to the signs of beating which we believe leads a little bit over into the identification issue, the prisoners were very clear that they had visible signs of bleeding, of being beaten, blood on the floor, swollen eyes, et cetera, and that can be confirmed through the testimony of confidential witness 007. You also heard from Mitrovic, and he said when he was in the hall way he observed the prisoners and they bore the signs of having been beaten. The Defence challenged the witness Branimir Mitrovic, challenged his recollection of the fact on the basis that he was seven years old at the time. Your Honour, I submit to you that indeed a seven year old remembering having played with a specific playmate at the age of seven or what kind of game he played at seven may not be something he can recollect 12 years later. But a seven year old, Your Honour, who observed prisoners being beaten on a daily basis during the time that he was in Srebrenica is not something a seven year old or anyone else is likely to forget, Your Honour. And in fact, when his recollection was challenged by the Defence, he was adamant that he remembered the circumstances. And he remembered them, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits, because they were unique and people do remember incidents because of that, because it's outside of their every day normal experience. And that is true, Your Honour, with respect to Branimir Mitrovic. The lighting conditions, you heard confidential Witness 007 and other witnesses talked about the fact that they were beaten in a cell and, yes, it was dark but they also testified that there was light used by lighting bits -- by the attackers using lighting bits of paper that created light and you heard this from more than one witness, Your Honour, and I submit to you that this is not a fact that would have been fabricated. Your Honour, Naser Oric, the Prosecution has alleged, visited the prison, as did his deputy, Zulfo Tursunovic. The Prosecution submits that the evidence of Ilija Ivanovic is credible and this is evidence, Your Honour, that was challenged by the Defence repeatedly regarding the witness's identification of Naser Oric as well as the circumstances under which he was beaten, followed by Naser Oric -- the ability -- followed by the exact circumstances, Your Honour, of who was in the room when he was taken to the reception area. You may recall that Mr. Ivanovic said he had been beaten, he was taken to this room, and you recall he -- recalled that he testified that he was familiar with Ahmo Tihic, whom he recognised. He also testified that he was familiar with Zulfo Tursunovic, and he said Mandza was also present in the room. And he said that there was a man that he later recognised as Naser Oric, and I would at this point, since there has been so much discussion on this issue, I would like to refer to the transcript where Mr. Ilija Ivanovic testified to these events, and that is transcript 4050, line 20. Question: "Did there come a point in time where you were removed from the cell and taken to another room in this building to be questioned?" Answer: "Yes, I remember once, can't say whether it was more than that. They took me to the reception room where they had the soldiers who watched us. I was taken out of the room and taken to the reception room. I recognised Ismet. He was a person I noticed, also Tihic, Ahmo Tihic, and Ismet he referred to is Ismet Odic. I found out who the others were later on and their names. There were five persons there for sure, up to seven. I'm not sure if this was recorded or not but it's not important. I saw one man, a bearded, dark, a bearded man, dark. I can't say that I knew Naser Oric but when we returned to the cell after this brief interrogation the soldiers told me, did you see our Dela, Naser? Some of them said Naser, some of them said, the boss. I didn't know the man though. I can't say it was that man." Later on, Your Honour, you may recall Mr. Ivanovic testified about having seen, having recognised this person from the reception room, from that event. Transcript 4055, it was a result of -- I'll rephrase. Your Honour put this question to the witness, line 11: "So if someone presented to you with a person and told you this is Naser Oric, you wouldn't have been able to confirm that because you did not know the man?" The witness responded, Mr. Ilija Ivanovic responded: "I'm not even saying that I did see him on TV several times later but I can't say something that is just not true. I didn't know him at the time. Because I had known him he would have been very easy for me to identify then." Judge Agius stated: "So and who did you see later on TV several times?" The witness responded: "No, what I'm saying is that although I saw him on TV several times I do not want to add something that I didn't actually know at the time. That's what I'm trying to say."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "But are you telling us that on TV later on you saw Naser Oric several times?" The witness answered: "Yes, in the newspapers and on TV." Your Honour, the Defence may seek to twist and turn that bit of evidence and testimony and on cross-examine the issue was revisited. But the witness was clear. He was honest. He didn't know Naser Oric the day he saw him in the reception room. He was clear. He saw him, he recognised him later on from television and the newspaper. The others, Your Honour, such as Zulfo Tursunovic, visited the prison and the witness recalled that as well. Mandic was someone who was present at the exchange. Ratko Nikolic testified that he recognised Naser Oric and just bringing you back a bit to the testimony of Ratko Nikolic who said that on his way to Srebrenica, sitting in the van was Zulfo Tursunovic who he later saw on a daily basis visiting the prison. And he testified that the person in the van he believed to be Naser Oric because of how they were treating him and how they referred to him. And you can refer to Prosecution's response paragraph 90 on that issue. He also testified that he later recognised there person from the newspaper. Stana Stamenic testified Naser Oric came to the cell and actually spoke to her and introduced himself, and you may find that reference to this conversation that he had with her in transcript 6618 to 620, and 6672 to 6673. Naser Oric told her he was the commander. Zulfo also visited the prison, she testified, and introduced himself and asked whether they had been mistreated. Milena Mitrovic, I'm sure we all recall that testimony because Ms. Mitrovic seemed to be confused about the last name of the individual and she summed up that she recalled the last name to be Kolic. The Prosecution submits that in fact that last name was Naser Oric that was told to her and her memory failed her on that regard and she said Kolic. But that's what she remembered and she was honest about that. When the Defence sought to cross-examine her on where she saw this individual, after a series of questions, it was clear that she saw him in the prison and not in the police station as the Defence may have -- or as the Defence was trying to elicit from her, the Prosecution believes. Your Honour, the Prosecution -- Naser Oric had knowledge of prisoners and we believe that that has been briefed in our closing brief as well as our reply brief. But if we could just play a bit of his interview regarding the matter of prisoners and Zulfo Tursunovic.
