utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to put your mind at rest, Ms. Richardson, we already have, at least twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, Your Honour. Your Honour, the identification issue, as posited by the Defence, as briefed in their closing brief is one that I would like to address the Trial Chamber at this point. The Prosecution is of -- the Prosecution submits that the evidence regarding the identification or recall, as we would refer to it, as the recognition of Naser Oric, was sufficient for the Court to find beyond a reasonable doubt that he was in the prison, that he did observe the physical appearance of the prisoners, and as such he was put on actual notice and inquiry notice and had a duty to prevent and punish. It's the Prosecution's position that the Defence has replied -- erroneously sought support in the Tribunal jurisprudence as well as Turnbull, which I will address in a moment. The Defence states that the law on identification evidence does not allow a finding that Oric was identified at the crime site, and we submit that that is incorrect. It's The Prosecution's position that the jurisprudence referred to by the Defence does not support this claim at all, in particular the evidence in Oric -- in the case of Naser Oric is very different in nature from the case cited by the Defence. And we submit that it's altogether much safer, facts, and facts and circumstances in this case than in the cases referred to by the Defence. In both the detention facility, that being the prison, as well as the prison, Your Honours, prisoners confirm either that they knew Naser Oric before in the case of Mrs. Sarac who told Mr. Radic, and in the case in the second scenario where you have this Stana informing Milena Mitrovic that that's Naser Oric and we have Naser Oric introducing himself to Stana Stamenic. We have Ilija Ivanovic recognising Naser Oric later on. We submit that these facts are different in nature from that raised by the Defence. Distinguishing the jurisprudence referred to by the Defence, the Prosecution will draw the Court's attention to Kupreskic where in Kupreskic the eyewitness identification was an issue with regard to two distinct incidents. In both incidents the conviction hinged upon the testimony of a single eyewitness. In one case the Appeals Chamber acquitted and in the second it upheld the conviction for both Kupreskic incidents the evidence was significantly weaker than in this case, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits. With regard to the first of these incidents, the only evidence placing the Kupreskic brothers at the crime scene was the testimony of Witness H. Witness H, whose testimony was unsafe for a large number of reasons including prior inconsistent testimony -- statements of the witness and contradictions between the statement of the witness and another eyewitness. The other eyewitness raised the distinct possibility that witness H identification of her neighbours in the attack had been a gradual development in months following the April 1993 atrocity. Now, with regard to the second incident in Kupreskic, this was the only incident placing Josipovic at the precise crime site and the witness's testimony was found sufficient on trial and on appeal, Your Honour. This finding was made despite discrepancies between -- in the witness's testimony itself. She testified that she had -- she had testified to have seen together with Josipovic two others and who were found to have been elsewhere at the time of the incident. Apart from this testimony, the only other factor -- the only other factor the appeals found in favour of conviction was the testimony was -- found that this testimony was generally corroborated by a witness who had seen Jusipovic attacking in the vicinity but not on the crime scene. The evidentiary situation, Your Honour, in Oric is not comparable to the situation in Kupreskic. In Kupreskic it was only one eyewitness who existed for each incident. By contrast Naser Oric had been identified in both detention facilities by a number of witnesses, many of whom had an opportunity, and we submit that this was not a fleeting glance as suggested but an opportunity, a fair amount of time, to recognise him later on. And we have also talked about the fact that he was known to a particular witness, Mr. Sarac. The identification in the present case again was not based on fleeting glances, obstructing views or viewing in the dark because as you recall, Mr. Ivanovic testified that he saw Naser Oric in the reception room area. Stanic Ivanovic said he came into the cell and she had a good view of him. And Your Honour it is based on mutually corroborated evidence from all of the witnesses who had repeated opportunities to observe Naser Oric that the Prosecution submits was sufficient for a finding that Naser Oric was in the prison and reliable. In sum, Your Honour, Kupreskic cannot possibly support the Defence's position that Naser Oric was identified as unsafe. In other words, Your Honour, this is not the same situation. In this case the finding of the Court of the Trial Chamber would not be unsafe. In Kunarac, the decision in Kunarac referred to by the Defence, explicitly clarifies that all comments to which the Defence refers are made for the case that the evidence end quote the evidence of the witness is the only evidence given in relation to that fact -- Your Honour, the Defence also erroneously --

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do apologise. The Defence uses the case of Turnbull, and Your Honours were provided copies of this decision, erroneously again, that they -- that the Defence has --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. The Defence has relied on Turnbull to support its position that the identification is unreliable and, again, Your Honour, the same holds true with regards to the distinction in the cases. The decision of the Court of appeals of England and Wales in Turnbull, the Prosecution submits, if anything it supports the Prosecution's position rather than the Defence. The most relevant finding in Turnbull was that if apart from the poor identification evidence there is other evidence which goes to support the correctness of the identification, a conviction may be entered. Turnbull decided three appeals based on identification. It upheld one conviction and reversed two. Turnbull's conviction was upheld despite the only identification witness only briefly saw Turnbull's face. The verdict could not be said to be unsafe because the identification witness already knew Turnbull from previous times. And that there was some corroboration for this identification. The same holds true, Your Honour, in this case, that the Stana pointed out Naser Oric to the Milena Mitrovic and Mr. Sarac testified that he knew Mr. Oric from before and he conveyed this information to Mr. Radic. The other two cases referred to in the Turnbull identification -- the other two identifications which were found to be unreliable because of very poor identification evidence, Your Honour. In one case, both witnesses did not know the assailant before the attack. The attack itself during which the assailant could be observed was over a few moments. The crime scene was a dark alley. A different witness identified a very different looking person and the description of the assailants originally given by the witness were contradictory. In the other case the persons were seen by the witness wore a Balaclava. One witness only saw him from the rear and the other one had given before the identification parade a description which in no way fit the description of the appellant or the accused. In both cases -- there was no further supporting evidence. Your Honour, again, the evidence in this present case is different. Consistent, mutually corroborative evidence about Naser Oric being present in the detention facilities even introducing himself by name has been provided in both prison scenarios and provided a number of witnesses had an opportunity, more than one, to see and observe him. The Defence -- the Prosecution would like to just make one small point with regards to the Defence's reliance on the use of the Devnis [phoen] report. The Defence claims that the Devnis report defines recognition evidence as seeing someone the witness already knows. This is wrong, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits. The report in paragraph 4.1 defines recognition as depending upon the human ability to memorise a face, if the memory is clear enough, it will enable a positive identification to be made." Thus the report's distinction between recognition and resemblance evidence simply distinguishes the quality -- simply distinguishes the quality of the witness's memory. Your Honour, the Prosecution would also highlight additional jurisprudence to the Court regarding identification that has already been established in our jurisprudence. We invite the Court to visit the Florenzija [phoen] Appeals Chamber judgement and there the Trial Chamber upheld the trial -- the -- here the Appeals Chamber upheld the Trial Chamber's treatment of witness identification evidence. There, the witness stated that she recognised the accused from television. She also identified the accused's voice as belonging to a person she encountered at two different locations. This evidence was in fact the only evidence that placed the accused at one of the locations. However, it was not the only evidence from this witness, nor from other witnesses, that identify the accused. The witness also testified that other people addressed the accused using his name in her presence. The same is true. Mr. Ilija Ivanovic, as I stated prior, came back from the receptionist room and the guards were asking him, "Did you see Naser?" "Did you see our boss?" Excuse me. "Did you see our Naser and boss?" The witness also testified that her encounter with the accused was -- excuse me I'll restate that. Her identification of the person she saw on television, she recall, was -- her identification was of the person she saw on television, Your Honour, not of the person she physically encountered. The Trial Chamber, however, accepted the witness's recognition but the person she saw on television was indeed the person she physically encountered, and she noted that he had put on weight. The Appeals Chamber held that this treatment of the witness's evidence, together with evidence of other identification evidence, made it reasonable for the Trial Chamber to have been satisfied that the accused had been identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We will get back to you with the date and we do apologise for not having it beforehand. Your Honour, that would essentially conclude my submission with respect to the identification issue. Recognition, identification, is, as knowledged by the Defence, the best form of visual identification, and recognition evidence has indeed been the basis of the identification of Naser Oric by the Prosecution witnesses, Your Honour. You may recall that Mr. Glikic testified that Naser Oric was at one of the exchanges and the exchange where prisoners were exchanged and the Prosecution submit that the -- particularly the men were visibly beaten. You may also recall the evidence where Naser Oric had taken out Sarac to negotiate with the Serb authorities regarding the exchange of Serb prisoners as Ms. Sellers referred to earlier. And I would just like to remind the Trial Chamber of the evidence of Slavoljub Filipovic and Mr. Okanovic who both testified that they -- specifically with regard to Mr. Filipovic who said that he recognised the voice of Naser Oric because he knew him from before and he spoke to him over the radio. And the Prosecution has extensively dealt with this in their Prosecution -- in the Prosecution's final brief and I would like to draw the Court's attention to Mr. Okanovic who recalls the code name of Mr. Naser Oric being Gazda and that he knew that because of what the other -- how he was -- how Gazda was treated when he was on the radio itself. And this is -- that this Gazda was Naser Oric based on what the other operators had said. And this, Your Honour, we believe -- we believe, is additional evidence of Naser Oric's knowledge of prisoners, as he talked about, discussed the wife of Filipovic and the capture of the children. Your Honour, I would like to move next to the exchange involving who the Prosecution submits was confidential witness 007 and there has been a lot from both sides on this issue regarding who was present at the exchange and how it actually proceeded. The Prosecution stands by its position in the Prosecution's closing brief, and also in the Prosecution's reply brief. Now, the Defence has indicated that Mr. Tucker, Colonel Tucker, should not be relied upon as having been present when Naser Oric brought out this prisoner and released him to the UNPROFOR individuals, but Colonel Tucker, and I believe that -- we sufficiently addressed this in the Prosecution's brief, remember very well that incident that he was, General Morillon was approached by Naser Oric who came along in a black Mercedes and had taken them to a place where C-007, who we believe any way, is C-007, Colonel Tucker didn't know who this person was but brought out this Serb prisoner to them. Now, the Prosecution concedes that Colonel Tucker may not have been correct in some aspects of that testimony, but the Prosecution stands by Colonel Tucker's testimony about what was important at the time, and what we believe is the most relevant portion of that evidence is that Naser Oric was the one who brought the prisoner out. Now, Colonel Tucker mentioned, testified - excuse me - that there may have been some bandages on the individual and as the videotape was shown, taken by Tony Birtley of the exchange itself, it was evident at least from the portion of the video we saw, that the prisoner did not have bandages on him, at least from what we were able to see. But I would take Your Honour to the portion of the testimony with respect to Colonel Tucker, and I think from reading his testimony it will be clear, and I'm not going to read it out because I think we are probably going to start running short on time. But Colonel Tucker did mention -- said he -- "I think" - I'm quoting from 6178 - "I think he had some bandages on his face. It was difficult to tell because his face was so dark and he had" -- "his face was so dark and he had obviously not shaved, but I think he had bandages as well." To Judge Brydensholt's question: "On the face, on the head? Do you recall anything about this? Where it was?" Colonel Tucker answered, "I can't remember where on his body the bandages were. What I do remember is that for some reason we had soldiers pull up his shirt or whatever, to look at his stomach because there was some -- I can't remember the reason why we looked at his stomach I don't recall the reason why." The Defence -- thank you. And, Your Honour, just would like to give the Court the information Your Honours sought before about the Limaj judgement, and that is November 30th 2005. Your Honour, Colonel Tucker may have been as well mistaken about who was present and we saw Colonel Dudley on the tape. Unfortunately the tape was not shown to Colonel Tucker. It may have refreshed his memory somewhat about who was present but he said -- Colonel Dudley was there, but at first he certainly intimated that he wasn't sure about all of the individuals present and upon being questioned again and again, he said, well, he's pretty sure that Dudley was present -- was not present, excuse me. In any event, Your Honour, the Prosecution would submit that Colonel Tucker had significant more information about this prisoner than Dudley or Birtley. In fact, Birtley did not take the whole incident, as the Defence would have you believe, and I would refer to transcript 15124 and this is on questioning on examination-in-chief to Mr. Birtley. Now finally a moving question -- now finally I'm moving on to two more topics, do you remember being present when a Serb prisoner or detainee was released? The answer: "Yes, I do." "And did you film at least part of that scene?" Answer: "Yes, I did." I would emphasise, Your Honour, the question was, "did you film at least part of the scene?" The answer was: "Yes, I did." Next question: "And do you remember how you came to be at the scene, the handover?" "I remember exactly. There was so much going -- I don't -- excuse me, I can't remember exactly. There was so much going on. I think I came across it by accident or I was told. I can't say with any degree of certainty." And that was Tony Birtley's testimony about the taping of the events. The Prosecution would submit to you, Your Honour, that in fact because Tony Birtley had only sudden appeared accidently that he did not see Naser Oric and that Naser Oric may very well have left by the time Tony Birtley began filming. And with respect to Colonel Dudley, who was not actively involved in the exchange, nor in any type of communication with Naser Oric, said Naser Oric was not present. Even though he's never met Naser Oric, he seemed to have wanted to supply the Trial Chamber with what the Prosecution submits is a little bit more information that -- than he had actual knowledge of, and he himself said that he was not part of the initial exchange, he was standing with the UNPROFOR soldiers and they said they needed help with a stretcher. Your Honour, again we submit that Colonel Dudley does not have the knowledge that he was -- that Tucker had, of the events, and we submit that it's quite possible that Dudley also appeared after the prisoner -- after Naser Oric had possibly left. Now, I would, in addition to what Colonel Tucker said about the exchange of the prisoner -- I would like to draw your attention to the portion of his testimony where he talked about the fact that Naser Oric knew about the additional -- that there were two additional prisoners and he referred to his diary, and I would point to -- lead the court to trial transcript 5929, after just having -- reading out information on his diary, Colonel Tucker said "We released" -- he's quoting, "We released a wounded Serb prisoner. We know of two more Serbs held by Bosnian forces Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Srebrenica who's commanding -- whose commander is trying to get released." And he's reading a portion of his diary about that information that was placed in it. My answer to the question of what else was in his diary, he said, "My recollection is that Colonel Oric said that he had two more prisoners. General Morillon was pressing him, 'How many prisoners do you have? Don't hold on to them. Release them.' Then he said that he had two more but that they were common criminals and nothing to do with fighting." Question: "And when had that conversation taken place to the best of your recollection?" "That" -- answer: "That morning." Question: "So when the prisoner was brought out?" Answer: "Bear in mind that it was General Morillon who told me this. I did not hear this myself. It was General Morillon who told me that he had been told that this morning." But, Your Honour, clearly this was significant enough for Colonel Tucker to put it in -- for it to be documented and it is corroborative of confidential witness 007 who said: "He left two prisoners back, who remained there, and those two prisoners was Jakov Dokic and a man from Zenica." Your Honour, we believe that Colonel Tucker's diary supports and corroborates that there were two prisoners left, and Naser Oric knew about them. I am drawing close to the end of my submission on this issue. Just a moment, Your Honour.

And this is not new jurisprudence, Your Honour, it's been said many times of 7(3) liability. And this knowledge, Your Honour, the requirement of knowledge can be proven direct or circumstantially and I don't need to seem to lecture Your Honours on the law, but I would only add that the actual knowledge we believe was proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Naser Oric in fact had direct knowledge and knew that the prisoners had -- were subjected to cruel treatment and had been beaten and failed to prevent further beatings as well as the deaths of the prisoners. We would also conclude that he had inquiry notice as well, and that his deputy Zulfo Tursunovic was in the prison, and that he had reason to know or should have been put on notice that there was a need for further investigation based on what happened in the first prison scenario, Your Honour, and based on what he himself observed in the prison. We proved beyond a reasonable doubt that he was in the prison and he failed to prevent or punish.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll be addressing you next and it goes to the issue of Naser Oric's 7(3) responsibility throughout the time period of our indictment, which is from 1992 until 1995. Your Honours, effective control means that one has to have reasonable means, material ability, to effectively control subordinates but control that specifically goes to preventing the commission of crimes and if those crimes were unfortunately committed and we certainly use committed in its larger sense, aided and abetted, committed, in any way participated in, that that superior then has to punish those crimes. The Trial Chamber has heard a lot of testimony concerning inability in Srebrenica in 1992-1993, to do anything, to set up any system, to have a War Presidency, to have a military police, to have any type of functioning court system. The Prosecution submits that failing to prevent and failing to punish does not need a judicially sanctioned means such as a formal court, or even a formal, judicially sanctioned superior. Your Honours, I take you to the Blaskic appeals decision where indicators of effective control are more a matter of evidence than substantive law and indicators are limited to showing whether the accused had the power to prevent, punish or initiate measures leading to proceedings against alleged perpetrators. I'm quoting from the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement of the 29th of July 2004, paragraph 69, because the Prosecution puts before Your Honours that the situation in Srebrenica in 1992, 1993, 1994, might not have permitted Tuzla or Sarajevo to come down and give the absolute legal seal of approval on every military institution, including military courts, but that does not leave the subordinates in Srebrenica outside of the law, outside of military law, outside of even discipline. Your Honours, the superiors within Srebrenica knew that there were legal limits and that going across such barriers could incur punishment. Naser Oric says in his suspect interview that one of the first things he did was to issue an order about not burning and during the interview, I believe he contacted Mr. Mazic to confirm if that order had been issued and it appears that it has. We never saw the order brought before this Trial Chamber. We never saw one Defence witness asked whether he remembered that order coming out. We heard so much that there was no paper. Well, it would have been good if there had been an order because the paper that could have been sacrificed in writing this order certainly was worth it or even if it was transmitted orally, via communications, Motorolas, in meetings, that would have at least shown that he took the reasonable measures that he materially had available to him to prevent. We have never seen a discussion in P84 about a standard [inaudible] not to destroy, wantonly destroy, the property after attack. What we have seen instead in P84 is omission of that discussion or we have a situation where we see a warning, "Burn after we have finished or burn after there has been a collection of goods." Now, the Prosecutor did not charge Naser Oric with the attacks in Skelani but I would take to you P84, new P84.1, and I have page 50, "Skelani was burned." The discussion at the OS Staff meeting that was held on the 10th of January 1993, and this is an OS Staff meeting, not a joint War Presidency meeting, says "Skelani was burned, arson should not be allowed before people from Skelani take back their belongings." Almost to suggest that that criminal act is sanctioned after taking back belongings but not before. Your Honour, one might ask, then, why was there no discussion of "we do not burn Skelani. I've heard that there was been burning at other places, Fakovici, Bjelovac, Jezestica, the burning has to stop." No the burning is conditioned upon when people can go to take their goods back. Your Honour, that goes a long way to showing why Naser Oric did not prevent, nor punish. You do not prevent or punish something that you agree should happen or even if you're indifferent that it should happen, or as a matter of fact in pattern or policy it does. During 1992 up until the end of January Your Honours need look no further as to why he didn't use any available means to prevent this type of wanton destruction, because it was a choice. That doesn't mean that later on, in 1993, after the hundreds, after the thousands, after the tens of thousands, of refugees come into Srebrenica and the humanitarian crisis is becoming acute, in the Defence's terminology, the slow-motion genocide is rising, and then we have demilitarisation where many refugees now leave the area and where the organisational structure seems to confirm itself, become more complex, and not less complex. We have soldiers coming in from Cerska that now come under the 8th Operational Group. We have the different soldiers coming in from areas that have fallen but they are all in Srebrenica now, forming, reforming themselves into units, all subordinate to Naser Oric. We have the military police having been demilitarised. Now, the fact that Naser Oric didn't use the institution of the military police prior to demilitarisation for these types of crimes leaves a bit of a question mark. I'll return to that in a second. But during demilitarisation we have Hakija Meholjic who said, "I took over the police," took over what was probably the functioning civilian police. Even if he did take over the military police we have an institution of law enforcement. Hakija Meholjic said that if he had had information passed to him concerning crimes committed by the military he would have investigated, as he did on certain occasions. That's the situation of Emir Halilovic, the killing of the Serb family. It wasn't perfect but it was functioning. Omerovic now has a civilian court system that would look at some of the complaints that occurred from military members. That doesn't mean that the jurisdiction for war crimes which is now in the military district court in Tuzla has been usurped or taken over but it means there could have been a method, and there was a method of transmitting information to Tuzla even if people couldn't be held beyond three days, and that seems to be one of the impossibilities we hear, the information that they should be removed from the area as soon as possible or let it be known in a file in Tuzla, in Sarajevo, that these members of the military have committed crimes, was not done. If you recall, there was testimony concerning discipline of soldiers, information that was sent to Tuzla by a legal officer, Rasid and the information concerned disciplinary measures. Who was held temporarily? The information shows that there was some effort to discipline in the demilitarisation time period in Srebrenica, irrespective of the number of refugees, irrespective of the level of humanitarian crisis. Your Honours, it's because they chose not to turn their attention to crimes committed against Serbs that we do not show the evidence because there was no evidence of those military men being asked to explain what they did when they went to Jezestica or to Fakovici or to Gravica. Your Honours recall that the Prosecution has spoken quite often about a document referred to as P598 which we put forth as a type of war path of the various units. There is a Huso Juric, whose name appears throughout the document, and it seems apparent that if he was, if not one of the recorders, he was the person that went around to the different units to get the information. He asked the same question every time: Where did you attack? Where did you defend. You know, who were your men, what was your weaponry, and then afterwards there was a section where he gathers information about who might receive awards or not. He seemed to be working together with one of the morale officers. But he was collecting information. Among some of the information he collects is evidence that towns were burned, Jezestica was burned, people are thinking back over the history of their participation and they say in document 598, "burnt completely." Even at that very moment, 1993-1994, that information could have been passed to the Legal Officers that Naser Oric was employing at that time regarding discipline, to say, "Would you please look into this? I'm getting information back about these subordinates having burned during the attacks. Can I have more information, please? Can I please transmit this on?" Your Honours, that was not done and that was at a time period when he had access to more military members in the town of Srebrenica, without having to worry about the danger of going from one area to another area within the enclave. That wasn't done because that was never meant to be done. Naser Oric merely chose not to pursue the crimes against the Serbs -- committed, excuse me, committed against the Serbs. I referred earlier to the military police. At times the Defence would have you believe that there was no military police, that it had functioned at such a low level that it had only two or three rifles, as Akif Krdjic says in P84, "I need more rifles." Irrespective of that, Naser Oric acknowledges in his interview that there was a military police, there was that institution. He reported to Ramiz Becirevic. Mr. Omerovic, a witness that we called, who discussed a lot of the impossibility of the Court system does say on transcript 8465 that the military police including Mirzet Halilovic would go to different apartment buildings and forcibly mobilise military-aged men. This was prior, had to be prior, to Mirzet Halilovic being dismissed from the police. The military police could go out and round up people, force them to the front line. The military police in December kept a rather well structured military police book. There might be some mistakes or incidents in there that might leave a bit of questioning but it's a fairly remarkable document of organisation in the midst of a time period when there was not supposed to be any possibility of organization. But if one goes into the document and see what were the types of crimes that were being addressed, they were crimes about taking weapons, crimes about misappropriation of food, at times what might have been rather large quantities of food, particularly for Srebrenica, who desperately needed to share the food among the people who were there. Discussions about prisoners coming into town. And then we have documents relating to the military police that were in the different units. So even if the Srebrenica military police was too localised in Srebrenica and there weren't enough military members in Srebrenica who they could have investigated, we do know that military police, particularly after the reorganisation, were placed in the different units outside of Srebrenica. They could have asked their members there, sent reports, they did, concerning stolen weapons, stolen food. There were reasonable means available. Naser Oric had the material ability. He chose not to use it in 1992 and 1993 or 1994. Now, Your Honours, from Naser Oric's point of view, from his mentality, it could be just a question of priorities. International humanitarian law doesn't ask you to do the impossible but you're not allowed to weigh and balance your priorities and choose not to do anything. I'd like Your Honours to look at a small portion of Naser Oric's suspect interview, and this is coming up now, I believe, it's P329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes. The video starts at 3 hours 0 minutes and 39.2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it's transcript 21, page 6, line 42.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: "Explain to me when it happened. Just as you acknowledged the fact that you did address volunteers, okay, and would it not have been appropriate at that time, whenever you addressed volunteers, welcoming them to the course, or at any other occasion when you stood in front of them, to remind them of their obligations to behave in an appropriate fashion during their actions in the war? "Did you ever do that? Yes. I will give you an example now. When we were attacking this firing line, the line at Zvijezda, when you look from Potocari, it is above the Muslim village of Budak, B-u-d-a-k, before we set out we stood to see roughly how many volunteers had come. I went in front of them and I said to the fighters what was the reason for the attack and where we were attacking. I said that you know that we have people, Muslims, who are down in Konjevic Polje, that they have the same problems as we do, that the Chetniks are attacking us from all sides, that they are -- that they are threatened at this -- that they are threatened at the moment with complete destruction as they are being heavily attacked, and that if we were not -- if we didn't attack the firing lines at Zvijezda, sir, that -- and didn't draw attention to ourselves, all of these Chetniks on [indiscernible] would go to the area of Konjevic Polje and that we would have to take it at all costs in order to make it -- make it easier for them to lessen the Chetnik attacks because this point was the entry door to Bratunac. It was an extremely dangerous point. I asked -- I said to them if anyone is afraid, it's better that they leave now, better that he left now rather than that he went along and then be scared later on if someone trod on a mine or whatever, that we would have to take them back as well as our real fighters. I told them that this was a hill strewn with various kinds of mines and that it would be difficult to take it. I understand that but when you get to the point of my question -- was it at this occasion you said something in relation to discipline and their behaviour in battle? Because that's the only thing I need to know for this question so we can move on I don't understand how they behaved -- there is no rules of behaviour in a battle. You've got a gun, I've got a gun. The only rule is who is going to kill who first? Is that right? You shoot at me and I shoot at you? There is no language here, there is no speech. The only -- the only discussion is through barrels. Yes, but if one of us are wounded, not dead, if one of us -- wait a minute, and if one of us is taken prisoner, they are -- those are the rules my colleague is referring to. The commanders received orders and it wasn't for me now as a commander to go to each soldier and explain this to them. This was for the local commanders. They were responsible for carrying out -- They were responsible for carrying out the preparations with their groups, but upon an occasion like that when you had all the soldiers in front of you, surely you could have taken the opportunity to remind them of their responsibilities. Yes, I did. I told them that they had to behave in a military way, and you can understand everything from that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the video was stopped at 3 hours 07 minutes 39.8 seconds. Yes, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours I'll conclude on this section by stating that Naser Oric couldn't allow demilitarisation could equate impunity and if he gave his local commanders orders, which he says he did, then he was alerted that if crimes occurred he should have punished them. He's also alerted if he gave the order not to burn, that he had a duty to prevent crimes. Your Honour, Naser Oric had effective control, he's probably one of the few military officers whose staff wants to resign because he's not using his effective control. Please use it. They are pleading with him to use the power he has. He had the power, he had the reasonable means, the material ability. He chose not to prevent or punish the crimes against the Bosnian Serbs who are the subjects of our amended indictment. Right now we are going to hear a bit about the hostile witnesses and then we will conclude our closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that will be Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, if Your Honours please. I won't trouble you for long on this issue. The points I can make -- I want to make can be made briefly. I want to address some comments to you about the witnesses in this case. By now you have heard all and many arguments from the Defence and the Prosecution concerning credibility, reasons why you should believe some witnesses, disbelieve others, and so on. I certainly am not going to get into that. In the main I want to deal with the issue of hostile witnesses. Before I proceed any further, though, there is just one brief matter that I want to raise. The Defence criticised the Prosecution for its approach to their witnesses, and commented on the Defence -- on the Prosecution motivations for criticising witnesses. You'll find those references at paragraphs 92, 94, 100, and 101 of the Defence reply. I'm not going to read out what is said. All I can say to you -- all I want to say to you about that is this: If Your Honours please, the -- any criticisms that the Prosecution has made of Defence witnesses spring from forensic issues and no other considerations. Hostile witnesses, if Your Honours please. The Defence suggests that the Prosecution decision not to treat Nedret -- Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic as a hostile witness requires the Prosecution to accept his damaging testimony as a concluded fact, a conceded fact. The Prosecution's submission to you is that this position is wrong, clearly wrong, and it's not sustained by anything that the Defence has argued or put to you in its briefs, in their reply, or in their closing brief. The crux of the matter lies in paragraph -- sorry, footnote 29 of the Defence closing brief, where they deal with -- in fact, at that point they are dealing with the evidence of Hakija Meholjic and two points emerge from footnote -- the all important footnote 29. That's what I'm going to be speaking to you about. Two points emerge from the -- from that footnote. Firstly, it is said that there is a general principle that a party cannot impeach its own witness and, secondly, the reason for that is that a party guarantees his own witness's credibility and a party is morally bound by the testimony of his own witness. And as authority for those propositions, the Trial Chamber is referred to an article appearing in the Toronto Law Journal, the author, Mr. Bryant, entitled "The Common Law Rule Against Impeaching One's Own Witness." Before I look at the article, I urge Your Honours to remember the wording of the footnote. It is a general principle of law and one recognised by this Tribunal. No authority is provided to you, none at all, on why that should be so and why it is that the following principles are recognised by this Tribunal. The -- what the Defence is really seeking to do here, if Your Honours please, is not to -- what they are really concerned about is not to establish that the Defence can't impeach its own witnesses. There has been no attempt on the part of the Prosecution to do that, in any event. What the Prosecution -- what the Defence really seek to do here is to ensure or ask you to accept that the Prosecution is morally bound and must guarantee everything Mujkanovic said, including his damaging testimony. And they rely, as I said, on the article. The important thing for you to do in the Prosecution's submission, is to go to the article and it's been provided to Your Honours. I think you have full copies of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not going to take you through it. It's an interesting article and deals with the history of the common law rule against impeaching one's own witnesses except where they are declared hostile. And it's apparent from reading the article that the author makes clear that the rule against impeaching one's own witnesses is developing constantly in the common law world and you can see that, for instance, at page 431 of the article, where it describes the developments that occurred in the 19th century and the changing and evolving positions of the rule. I don't intend to take you through it but there is a discussion of colleges case and a discussion of developments between 1800 and 1850, where -- and the author notes, in the period between 1800 and 1850 the rule appeared more frequently in the reported cases and it became clear that the mere fact of having called a witness will not preclude a party from proving the truth of any particular fact material to the issue by any other competent testimony though such evidence may be in direct contradiction to what the witness may have testified. That's just one reference to one period of the developing and evolving rule. So that the central submission I make is that what springs out at you from this article is that it's not a static rule and it differs, indeed, from common law jurisdiction to common law jurisdiction. Furthermore, and I don't need to dwell on this, Your Honours have made pronouncements throughout this trial and the law and jurisprudence of this Tribunal is redolent with observations that you are not bound by the Rules of Evidence springing from domestic jurisdictions or national jurisdictions. However, if you go to the actual quote itself, that is contained -- that is extracted and placed in footnote 29, it's clear that the Defence failed to cast their eye as far as the beginning of the sentence that they quote and they failed to cast their eye into the sentence below. The pronouncement -- the quotation is an extract of a sentence at the top of page 433. There you can see those words, a party guarantees his own witness's general credibility and a party is morally bound by the testimony of his own witness. What precedes the sentence, though, is this: The admission of this evidence conflicts with two of the traditional reasons given in support of the rule. A party guarantees his own witness's general credibility and a party is morally bound by the testimony of his own witnesses -- of his own witness. Wigmore, which I believe is a well known North American text on evidence, states that the reception of this evidence signifies the rejection by the Courts of those justifications for the rule. This article is in no way support for the proposition advanced in footnote 29. It's emphatic and it's surrounded by words that make that clear. So the reliance that the Defence places on this article is unfounded. The issue, though, if Your Honours please, has been looked at and pronounced upon, not precisely this issue of witnesses said to be hostile but the assessment of witness evidence has been pronounced upon in the Appeals Chamber in the Kupreskic decision of the 23rd of October 2001, at paragraphs 332, 333, and 334, where the Appeals Chamber said, and I should quote, it's only brief, and I can't put it any better. "It is of course open to a Trial Chamber and indeed any Tribunal of fact to reject part of a witness's testimony and accept the rest. It is clearly possible for a witness to be correct in her assessment of certain facts and incorrect about others." And then at paragraph 333, "The jurisprudence of this Tribunal confirms that it is not unreasonable for a Tribunal of fact to accept some but reject other parts of a witness's testimony. The situation before the Appeals Chamber in the present case is akin to those cases within the jury system where a jury returns different verdicts on different counts even though the evidence for all counts comes from one witness." And then in paragraph 334, the Appeals Chamber says, "The Appeals Chamber has reiterated the importance of such a holistic approach to assessing credibility within its own jurisprudence. A Tribunal --" and referring to the Tadic case, "A Tribunal of fact must never look at the evidence of each witness separately as if it existed in a hermetically sealed compartment. It is the accumulation of all the evidence in the case which must be considered. The evidence of one witness when considered by itself may appear at first to be of poor quality but it may again strength from other evidence in the case." That's the approach that the Prosecution urges upon you. You are entitled to, and you should, and you are free to, look at the evidence of Dr. Mujkanovic in the light of all the other evidence in the case and you're free to reject parts of it, accept parts of it, accept none of it, accept all of it, whatever you wish as you are the triers of fact. So the -- and that approach, if the -- that approach, of course, the fact that you are free to do that vitiates against any tying of this court's hands by the suggestion that the Prosecution is morally bound to accept that position, guarantees that position. If that were so, this case would have ended after Dr. Mujkanovic had testified. So that's all I want to say to you about this issue. The proposition of law advanced by the Defence just hasn't got legs. It can't walk in the first place because it's not authority for what it's said to be. Those rules don't apply here in this particular Tribunal. You're free to decide what facts you choose to accept or reject and that is the approach that the Prosecution urges that you adopt in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Ms. Sellers? We have got four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And we will conclude within those four minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that because I have another at 2.15 and it is bound to last, I don't know how many hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: While there is so much more that one could say I think enough has been said. I think Your Honours have the evidence before you. You have the Accused before you. You have the pleadings from both parties before you. The Defence will make their submissions. Your Honours, if I would ask you to remember one thing, I would certainly say that oh, and then another thing and then another thing. It will be the totality of the evidence. I cannot give you one key. What I can advance is the following thought: When awards were to be given out, when people were to be rewarded in Srebrenica, as subordinates, in the armed forces, even under the 8th operational group, even those who were deceased, such as Mirzet Halilovic, they mention valiant victories in which the subordinates had taken place or participated, and for Mirzet Halilovic, they recounted Kravica and they said that he left Kravica bloody and burning. I want Your Honours to look at the picture on Sanction offered by Defence witness. It's P460. Your Honour, this was taken, if I understand correctly, by Philipp and I would like to finally pronounce one name correctly in this Tribunal -- Recklinghausen, I probably didn't do it correctly. Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask you to look at this carefully. Naser Oric with his well-armed, uniformed men on horse, and leave you with the understanding that Kravica, on the day that it was taken, was bloody and burning. And Your Honours, this is a victory shot. This is going back into where we were victorious, we destroyed with fire. It's celebrated. It is not evidence of punishment. Naser Oric did not prevent or punish the crimes against the Serb victims. Naser Oric should be shown to be guilty beyond a reasonable doubt because he declared victory over crimes. Your Honour, this will conclude the arguments from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Sellers and I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, Ms. Richardson. Two small things for when the Defence would have finished. I draw your attention to page 199 of your final brief. You make reference to P456, and use it to strengthen or to sustain one of your submissions. P456 was admitted orally on the 2nd of November 2004 only, however, to prove the existence of an armed conflict and for no other reason. That's one thing I wanted to point out to you. Then in paragraph 25 of your final brief, you mention or you allege or submit that there are 17 documents from the Sokolac collection that have been made use of by the Defence but you do not indicate which ones you are referring to. And then equally in paragraph 28, you make a statement that -- this is page 14, the Defence made extensive use of documents from the Drina Corps collection to assist the case but there is no indication as to which documents you are referring to. Basically there are no footnotes. We would like you to address this when you make submissions on Friday. Also, how you submit we should look at -- at the moment, I can't remember the exhibit number, but the Defence entered into the records a report from Dr. Fagel or by Dr. Fagel on various documents on which the name of Zanin Zananovic [phoen] appeared together with a signature next to the name, and apart from what Dr. -- from Zananovic himself stated in a statement that is also on the records, it seems to me, reading Dr. Fagel's report that there is barely one document that he has examined that he can attribute any measure of probability to Zananovic himself. So we would like to hear submissions on how you submit we should look at all those documents, some of which you mentioned this morning, like document P15, if I remember correctly, P15, P16, any way, there are several of them, quite a number. I leave you with that. I thank you so much for all your submissions. Tomorrow we'll start with your submissions, and then Friday, as we agreed will be dedicated to tying up the few loose ends that there will be. But if you need Monday as well, we are prepared to give you Monday. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
